title_en: Lin, Chen v. Cai — dispute over general personality rights

full_text_en:
Lin and Chen v. Cai — dispute over general personality rights

【Ruling Summary】

1. When civil subjects exercise their respective democratic rights, they shall do so within the limits granted by law and shall not infringe upon the lawful rights and interests of other civil subjects on the pretext of exercising their own rights.

2. When trying a case involving conflicts arising from the exercise of civil rights by different civil subjects, a people's court shall, based on the facts, determine the legality and appropriateness of each party's exercise of their civil rights, and thereby balance the aforementioned conflicts of rights.

Plaintiff: Lin, male, born on February 12, 1994, residing in Shantou City, Guangdong Province.

Plaintiff: Chen, female, born on July 20, 1993, residing in Shantou City, Guangdong Province.

Defendant: Cai, male, born on November 15, 1991, residing in Shantou City, Guangdong Province.

Plaintiffs Lin and Chen filed a lawsuit with the Haojiang District People's Court of Shantou, Guangdong Province, against defendant Cai regarding a dispute over general personality rights.

Plaintiffs Lin and Chen alleged: On June 2, 2016, Lin and Chen had a quarrel at the entrance of Xianshi Temple in Haojiang District, Shantou City. Without the consent of Lin and Chen, defendant Cai used his mobile phone to film their quarrel and uploaded the video to the Internet for dissemination. After learning of this, Lin and Chen demanded that Cai hand over the mobile phone used to film the video and delete the video, but Cai refused. Subsequently, the video spread rapidly on the Internet, causing Chen to have repeated suicidal thoughts due to unbearable social舆论 and "doxxing". On the evening of June 3, 2016, Lin and Chen reported the matter to the public security authorities. At the Da'hao Police Station of Haojiang Branch of Shantou Public Security Bureau (hereinafter referred to as Da'hao Police Station), Cai admitted that he had done the above and wrote a "Clarification Letter", expressing his agreement to delete the video. On June 24, 2016, the above video was broadcast by the Nightline 60 Minutes column of Anhui Television Station Public Channel (hereinafter referred to as Anhui Public Channel). Thereafter, the video was broadcast on major video websites and online news headlines, with the highest number of views reaching over 61,934,000. Cai's above actions seriously affected the reputation, privacy, work, life, and mental state of Lin and Chen, infringing upon their right to portraiture and causing serious damage to their reputation. Lin and Chen now file a lawsuit with the court, requesting: 1. Cai immediately and completely remove the existing video from the Internet and make a public apology on Shantou Television Station's "Today's Vision" column or in a well-known newspaper, as well as a written apology on online platforms such as QQ, WeChat, and Sina Weibo; 2. Cai compensate Lin and Chen for moral damages and reputation damages in the amount of RMB 20,000.

In support of their claims, plaintiffs Lin and Chen provided to the court: 1. Video materials and the "Clarification Letter"; 2. Police report receipt.

Defendant Cai argued: On June 2, 2016, the defendant saw plaintiff Lin beating plaintiff Chen near Xianshi Temple in Haojiang District, Shantou City. Out of a sense of justice, he used his mobile phone to film the above illegal act. Later, at the request of his colleague Wu, he sent the video to Wu via WeChat and then immediately deleted the video from his mobile phone. The video was uploaded to a WeChat group by Wu, not by the defendant to the Internet. Accordingly, the defendant had already apologized to Lin and Chen and sent candies to Lin's parents as an expression of apology. During the handling of this dispute at the Da'hao Police Station, he also wrote a "Clarification Letter" to Lin and Chen. On June 25, 2016, Lin and Chen informed him that the video had been broadcast by Anhui Public Channel. The defendant then contacted Anhui Public Channel by phone and email to request deletion of the video from the Internet but received no reply. The defendant believes that the video he filmed involving Lin and Chen was taken in a public place and does not infringe upon Lin and Chen's right to privacy. The video was not used for profit, so it also does not infringe upon Lin and Chen's right to portraiture. Moreover, the video did not capture Lin's face, and Chen's face was not clearly visible. The video contained no false, insulting, or defamatory content concerning the plaintiffs, so there was no act of disparaging Lin or Chen. The impact of the video's dissemination on the Internet was not significant, and the defendant's filming was done in the spirit of upholding justice as part of the campaign to build a civilized city; it was not illegal. Lin and Chen's claim for moral damages has no basis. As an ordinary citizen, the defendant cannot coordinate with relevant websites to delete the video in question. Therefore, the defendant requests the court to reject all of Lin and Chen's claims.

In support of his arguments, defendant Cai provided to the court a "Notice on the 'Two Uncivilized Phenomena Snap-and-Share' Activity".

The Haojiang District People's Court of Shantou, Guangdong Province, found the following facts at first instance:

Plaintiff Lin, while on a road in Haojiang District, Shantou City, got into a quarrel with plaintiff Chen and openly slapped Chen's face. Defendant Cai used his mobile phone to film the above act by Lin and Chen and uploaded the video to the Internet. The video was broadcast by Anhui Public Channel on June 25, 2016, under the title "Live footage: Woman repeatedly slapped by boyfriend". Lin and Chen subsequently requested Cai to delete the video. Cai issued a "Clarification Letter" to Lin and Chen, expressing his willingness to delete the video in question that he had filmed.

The Haojiang District People's Court of Shantou, Guangdong Province, held at first instance:

Civil subjects exercising their civil rights shall do so within the limits granted by law. The law also prohibits any right holder from infringing upon the lawful rights and interests of other civil subjects by exercising their own rights. The crux of the dispute between the parties in this case is essentially a conflict between the exercise of civil rights by different civil subjects. It is necessary to determine the legality and appropriateness of each party's exercise of their civil rights based on the facts of the case, so as to balance the aforementioned conflict of rights. Although plaintiff Lin and plaintiff Chen are husband and wife, Lin openly used violence to slap Chen's face in a public place. Lin's act was illegal and had already infringed upon Chen's personal dignity. Defendant Cai filmed and published the above illegal violent act by Lin; this was not improper. However, with respect to Chen, being violently slapped in the face in a public place already constituted an infringement of her personal dignity. By publishing the video without blurring Chen's facial features or image, causing the video to be broadcast on Anhui Public Channel, Cai's actions effectively expanded the adverse effects of the infringement of Chen's personal dignity, causing her greater mental harm. Cai shall bear corresponding tort liability for this.

Regarding plaintiff Chen's claim that defendant Cai's actions infringed upon her right to reputation, the court held that reputation is the comprehensive evaluation of a natural person's or legal entity's moral character, reputation, image, etc., by society. Infringement of the right to reputation refers to acts by which a perpetrator insults or slanders another's reputation through various means, leading to a lowering of the victim's social evaluation. Personal dignity, on the other hand, refers to the minimum social status that a "person" should have and the minimum respect they should receive from society and others. Although acts that infringe upon a citizen's right to reputation will, to varying degrees, damage the citizen's personal dignity, acts that infringe upon a citizen's personal dignity may not necessarily result in a lowering of the victim's social evaluation. Chen did not provide evidence to prove that Cai's actions had lowered her social evaluation. Moreover, Cai's actions did not constitute insults, defamation, or similar acts. Therefore, Chen's claim that Cai infringed upon her right to reputation lacks factual and legal basis, and the court does not support it. Regarding Chen's claim that Cai infringed upon her right to privacy and right to portraiture, since Lin and Chen's actions occurred in a public place and there is no evidence in this case that Cai obtained any benefit from the filming, Chen's claim lacks legal basis, and the court does not support it.

Regarding plaintiff Lin's claim that defendant Cai infringed upon his lawful rights and interests, since Lin openly used violence to insult another person in a public place, his act was itself illegal and prohibited by law. Cai's publication of Lin's illegal act was not improper. Moreover, the video only showed Lin's back, and an ordinary person could not identify him as Lin himself. Therefore, Cai's actions did not infringe upon Lin's lawful rights and interests. Lin's claim lacks factual and legal basis, and the court does not support it.

A person who causes damage to another's civil rights and interests through fault shall bear tort liability. Where a citizen's personal dignity is infringed upon, he or she has the right to demand cessation of the infringement, elimination of the effects, an apology, and may also claim compensation for losses. Defendant Cai published the video in question on the Internet, and it was broadcast by Anhui Public Channel, resulting in the video still existing on the Anhui Television Station website. Cai is obligated to notify Anhui Television Station to delete the video on its website. Regarding plaintiff Chen's request that Cai delete the same video from other websites, as she failed to provide evidence that the video exists on other websites, the court does not support Chen's request beyond the above scope. Chen's request for Cai to make an apology is in accordance with the law. The manner of apology shall correspond to the scope of impact of the infringing act. The court holds that Cai shall make a written apology, the content of which shall be subject to the court's review. Since Cai's act of infringing upon Chen's personal dignity inevitably caused mental harm to Chen, Chen's claim for moral damages is justified. Considering the scope, impact, and degree of fault of the infringement in this case, the court determines that defendant Cai shall compensate plaintiff Chen RMB 1,000 as moral damages. However, it should be noted that Chen's claim for RMB 20,000 is excessive, so the court does not support the portion exceeding the above amount.

Although defendant Cai claims that his act was an exposure of uncivilized behavior and was a just act, no right is absolute. When the law grants a right holder the freedom to exercise their rights, it also prescribes the necessary limits for exercising such rights. When exercising his lawful rights, Cai must observe appropriateness and shall not infringe upon the lawful rights and interests of others. Therefore, the court does not accept his defense.

Accordingly, the Haojiang District People's Court of Shantou, Guangdong Province, pursuant to Article 101 and Article 106, Paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 6, Paragraph 1, Article 22, and Article 36, Paragraph 1 of the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 42 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Protection of Women's Rights and Interests, Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 90 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment on August 30, 2016:

1. Defendant Cai shall, within ten days after this judgment takes legal effect, notify Anhui Television Station Public Channel to delete the video titled "Live footage: Woman repeatedly slapped by boyfriend" broadcast on June 25, 2016, that exists on its website.

2. Defendant Cai shall, within ten days after this judgment takes legal effect, submit to the court a written apology addressed to plaintiff Chen, the content of which shall be determined by the court; if overdue, the court will designate a nationally distributed newspaper to publish the main contents of this civil judgment, with the costs borne by defendant Cai.

3. Defendant Cai shall, within ten days after this judgment takes legal effect, pay plaintiff Chen RMB 1,000 as moral damages.

4. Reject the claim of plaintiff Lin.

5. Reject the other claims of plaintiff Chen.

If the obligation to pay money is not fulfilled within the period specified in this judgment, double interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance shall be paid in accordance with Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

Court acceptance fee of RMB 100 (already paid) shall be borne by defendant Cai.

After the first-instance judgment was rendered, neither party filed an appeal, and the first-instance judgment has taken legal effect.
